title: Building an AI-Ready America: Higher Education in the Age of AI
author: Michael B. Horn
summary: Michael B. Horn shares testimony prepared for a Congressional subcommittee on higher education and artificial intelligence, making the case that AI should be understood as infrastructure -- like electricity -- rather than as a tool or a threat. The testimony argues that higher education institutions are structurally unprepared for AI because they are organized around information scarcity (faculty as knowledge gatekeepers) in an era of information abundance, and because accreditation frameworks reward seat time rather than demonstrated competency. Horn's core policy recommendations include reforming accreditation to focus on outcomes rather than inputs, creating federal support for AI-integrated competency-based programs, and treating AI literacy as a general education requirement on par with writing and quantitative reasoning. The piece is notable for engaging Congress on the structural rather than the surface-level implications of AI for higher education.
points: * Horn frames AI as infrastructure -- comparable to electricity -- not as a tool or threat, arguing that this framing changes the policy question from 'how do we manage AI in classrooms?' to 'how do we rebuild institutions around an AI-infused world?' * Higher education is organized around information scarcity (faculty as knowledge gatekeepers) but AI creates information abundance -- the institutional model that made sense in 1960 is structurally misaligned with the 2026 reality. * Accreditation frameworks that reward seat time rather than demonstrated competency are the specific structural barrier to AI-ready education -- they make it nearly impossible for institutions to redesign around learning outcomes. * Horn's legislative recommendations include reforming accreditation to focus on outcomes, federal support for competency-based programs, and treating AI literacy as a universal general education requirement. * The piece is targeted at Congress because Horn's argument is that market forces and institutional initiative alone will not be sufficient -- the accreditation and financial aid infrastructure that shapes all U.S. higher education requires federal reform.
quotes: Think about electricity. We didn't ask whether electricity was good or bad for manufacturing. We asked how to rebuild manufacturing around electric power. The institutions that asked the wrong question -- is electricity safe? is it fair? -- got left behind. AI is the electricity of our era, and Congress is being asked the same question right now.

Higher education is organized around information scarcity. The professor knows things the student does not. The library has books you cannot find elsewhere. The credential signals that you sat in rooms with people who knew things. All of that made sense in 1960. Almost none of it makes sense in 2026.

Accreditation is the hidden hand that shapes everything downstream. As long as accreditation frameworks reward seat time rather than demonstrated competency, institutions cannot redesign around learning outcomes without risking their funding.

AI literacy is not an elective. It is a general education requirement. In 1960, we decided that every college graduate needed to be able to write an essay and reason quantitatively. In 2026, we need to decide that every college graduate needs to be able to work effectively with AI tools. That is not a high bar. It is the floor.

The market will not solve this fast enough on its own. The incentive structures in higher education are deeply misaligned with what students and employers need. That is a policy failure, and it requires a policy response.
